title: S3-like Object Storage
problem: Design a distributed, highly durable object storage service like Amazon S3 supporting PUT / GET / DELETE of arbitrary-size objects with versioning.
summary: A write-once, read-many blob system split into three planes: (1) a stateless REST API that speaks the S3 protocol, (2) a metadata service that maps object keys to the placement of their data chunks, and (3) a fleet of data nodes that store the actual bytes. The dominant design choice is separating metadata from data: the metadata service is a small, strongly-consistent index ("which chunks live on which data nodes"), while data nodes are dumb, horizontally-scaled storage units protected by erasure coding (Reed-Solomon 6+3) for 11 nines of durability at ~1.5x overhead rather than 3x full replication. The main tradeoff is EC's higher reconstruction cost on read tail and on single-node failure vs. 3x replication's simpler recovery. Versioning and deletes are tombstoned; a background garbage collector compacts freed space. Sized for Amazon-scale: trillions of objects, exabytes total, ~1M GETs/sec and ~100K PUTs/sec.

functional: PUT, GET, DELETE, HEAD, and LIST objects within a bucket
Multipart upload for objects larger than 100 MB
Object versioning with the ability to GET a prior version
Bucket- and object-level ACLs, signed URLs, and SigV4 auth
Consistent listing with pagination and prefix filters
Server-side encryption at rest and optional client-side keys
Lifecycle rules: TTL expiry, tiering to cold storage
nonFunctional: Scale to 10 trillion objects, 3 EB stored, ~1M GET QPS
P99 GET latency under 100 ms for small objects
Graceful degradation: single-AZ loss does not break reads

assumptions: 10 trillion objects stored lifetime, average object 200 KB (bi-modal: many small + few huge)
Durability target: 11 nines (99.999999999%) — one object lost per 10B per year
Availability target: 99.99% for GET, 99.9% for PUT (PUT tolerates slightly more retry)
Erasure coding scheme: Reed-Solomon 6+3 (6 data + 3 parity shards, tolerates 3 simultaneous shard losses)
Multipart upload threshold: objects > 100 MB split into 5–100 MB parts
estimates: PUT QPS: ~100K sustained, peak ~300K during backup windows
GET QPS: ~1M sustained, peak ~3M (analytics / ML training reads)
Bandwidth: 1M * 200KB ≈ 200 GB/s read egress from data-node fleet
Storage: 10T * 200KB * 1.5 (EC overhead) ≈ 3 EB raw, distributed across ~300K data nodes at 10 TB each
Metadata rows: 10T objects * ~1 KB each = 10 PB of metadata — sharded across ~10K metadata nodes
Multipart completes: 500K/day (assumes 5% of PUTs are large multipart)

client.name: Client (SDK / CLI / Browser)
client.summary: AWS SDK, s3cmd, or browser-based uploader speaking the S3 REST protocol over HTTPS.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Sign requests with SigV4 (HMAC-SHA256 over canonical headers)
- For objects > 100 MB: initiate multipart, upload parts in parallel, then complete
- Retry idempotent GETs on 5xx with exponential backoff
- Verify Content-MD5 / ETag on PUT responses

sections.heading: Multipart upload
sections.body:
```
InitiateMultipartUpload → upload_id
for part in chunks(5MB..100MB): UploadPart(upload_id, part_number, bytes) → ETag
CompleteMultipartUpload(upload_id, [{partN, ETag},...])
```
Parallelism of 8–32 parts is standard; a 5 GB object finishes in ~30s on a gigabit link.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: The SDK does a lot: partitioning, retries, signing, ETag checks. A naive curl upload will miss all of that and will silently corrupt large objects on a single TCP reset.

bottlenecks.title: Client uplink saturation on large multipart uploads
bottlenecks.trigger: Objects > 100 MB split into 5-100 MB parts with 8-32 parallel UploadPart streams; a 500 MB upload on a gigabit link takes ~3-8s and fully pins the client NIC
bottlenecks.symptom: PUT throughput plateaus well below backend capacity; other app traffic on the same host suffers latency spikes; multipart uploads of 5 GB objects take minutes instead of the expected ~30s
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tune SDK TransferManager: cap concurrent parts to min(8, cpu_count), set part_size adaptively (target ~10s per part at measured bandwidth), enable TCP BBR, and use S3 Transfer Acceleration or a regional endpoint closer to the client
bottlenecks.detection: Track SDK metric bytes_uploaded/sec vs nominal link capacity; alert when sustained upload throughput < 70% of link bandwidth during active multipart, or when p95 UploadPart wall time > 2x expected (part_size / bandwidth)

bottlenecks.title: Silent corruption / incomplete uploads without SDK-level integrity checks
bottlenecks.trigger: Raw curl or naive HTTP clients bypass SigV4 chunk signing, Content-MD5 per-part verification, and CompleteMultipartUpload ETag reconciliation — any TCP reset mid-stream on a 500 MB object can ack partial bytes
bottlenecks.symptom: GETs later return objects with wrong ETag, truncated parquet/zip files, or 400 BadDigest errors surfacing days after the write; multipart uploads stuck in pending state consuming quota
bottlenecks.mitigation: Mandate AWS SDK (or equivalent with x-amz-content-sha256 + Content-MD5 per part); enforce server-side by rejecting PUTs missing Content-MD5 > 5 MB; set bucket lifecycle rule to abort incomplete multipart uploads after 24h (matches upload_id expiry)
bottlenecks.detection: Monitor rate of 400 BadDigest / InvalidPart responses per client IP; alert on pending_multipart_rows growth > 1%/day or individual upload_ids older than 24h; client-side, fail loudly on ETag mismatch post-Complete

bottlenecks.title: Retry storms from unbounded GET backoff on 5xx
bottlenecks.trigger: With ~1M sustained GET QPS and peaks of 3M (analytics/ML reads), even a 0.05% server error rate means 500-1500 retries/sec per client fleet; naive exponential backoff without jitter synchronizes retries across workers
bottlenecks.symptom: Backend sees correlated retry spikes (thundering herd) after a transient API or data-node blip; client observes cascading timeouts and elevated p99 GET latency (>1s) despite 10ms service times
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use full jitter backoff (sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt))), cap retries at 3, set adaptive mode in SDK (aws-sdk retry_mode=adaptive) which adds client-side token-bucket rate limiting; respect Retry-After header from LB ejection
bottlenecks.detection: Track client-side retry_count histogram and retries_per_request ratio; alert when p99 retries > 2 or when retry_rate > 5% of total GETs over a 1-minute window; correlate with backend 5xx rate to catch synchronized patterns

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client is a real component here In most systems you draw the client as a thin arrow on the left and forget about it. For S3-like object storage, the client does actual work that the server *cannot* do on its behalf — and getting that work wrong corrupts data. Uploading a 5 GB video as a single HTTP PUT over a flaky connection will fail after 4.9 GB and force a full restart. So the SDK splits the object into 5–100 MB parts, uploads them in parallel, retries failed parts individually, and only then tells the server "here are the ETags, stitch them together." The server has no way to recover a broken single-shot stream — the client is where durability *starts*. ## What happens without it If a user uploads with raw `curl`, three things break. One, any TCP reset restarts the whole upload, so very large objects never complete on lossy networks. Two, without per-part MD5 verification, silent corruption surfaces days later when a GET returns a truncated parquet file. Three, the backend gets hammered: a 500 MB upload that dies at 90% and restarts burns ~1 GB of API bandwidth and 9 shard writes per data node per attempt, multiplied across the fleet during an outage. ## The numbers At 100K sustained PUT QPS with 5% being multipart (per the capacity notes: 500K multipart completes/day), that's ~5,000 multipart uploads happening *concurrently*. If each has 8–32 parallel part streams, the client fleet is juggling ~40K–160K concurrent TCP connections into the API tier. Pushing that coordination into the SDK keeps the API stateless — it just sees independent part PUTs. ## Trade-off The SDK is now a load-bearing dependency: a buggy or outdated client can silently violate contracts the server can't re-check.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer fronting the S3 API fleet, with anycast DNS for regional affinity.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Least-connections across healthy API replicas. TLS terminated here; plaintext HTTP to the API tier inside the VPC saves ~3–5ms per request.

sections.heading: Sticky per upload_id
sections.body: Multipart uploads benefit from session affinity — subsequent UploadPart calls route to the same API instance that cached the upload context, reducing metadata lookups. Implemented via consistent-hash on the upload_id query param.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: Multi-AZ HA pair, anycast VIP. A misbehaving API replica is ejected after 3 consecutive 5xx within 10s; the client sees one retry at most.

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU exhaustion at peak GET fan-in
bottlenecks.trigger: Peak 3M GET QPS + 300K PUT QPS = ~3.3M TLS handshakes/sec amortized across connection reuse; even with HTTP/2 keepalive at ~100 req/conn, that's ~33K new TLS sessions/sec to terminate. ECDSA handshake costs ~1-2ms CPU per connection — saturates LB cores before backend saturates.
bottlenecks.symptom: Client sees TLS handshake timeouts and `SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL`; p99 connection setup climbs from ~20ms to >2s while already-established connections still serve fine. Backend API fleet shows idle CPU — classic LB-pinned signal.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Offload TLS to dedicated hardware (AWS NLB with TLS listeners backed by Nitro, or F5/Netscaler); enable TLS 1.3 + session resumption (tickets) to cut handshakes ~80%; tune `ssl_session_cache` to 10M entries with 24h TTL; prefer ECDSA P-256 over RSA-2048 (~5x faster). Scale out LB layer horizontally via anycast — don't rely on a single VIP.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when LB CPU > 70% sustained for 5min, or when `ssl_handshake_latency_p99 > 100ms`, or when `new_tls_sessions_per_sec / total_requests_per_sec > 0.05` (indicates resumption failing).

bottlenecks.title: Connection concurrency cap on large-object streams
bottlenecks.trigger: Sim declares concurrency=50K per LB instance. With 200 GB/s read egress and ~5000 concurrent multipart uploads × 8-32 part streams each = 40K-160K concurrent TCP connections for PUTs alone, plus ~1M GET QPS at ~10ms service time = ~10K concurrent GETs. A single LB instance hits its file-descriptor or conntrack limit during peak.
bottlenecks.symptom: New connections rejected with `ECONNREFUSED` or silently dropped at SYN; existing long-lived multipart part uploads continue fine. On-call sees `nf_conntrack: table full` in dmesg or `accept4: Too many open files` in LB logs.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Raise `nf_conntrack_max` to 4M, `net.core.somaxconn` to 65K, ulimit nofile to 1M per LB node; shard traffic across ≥20 LB instances via anycast (each handling ~50K concurrent); use connection draining on health-check failure rather than hard-close to avoid retry stampedes.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `conntrack_used / conntrack_max` — alert at 70%; track `accept_queue_overflow` counter (TcpExtListenOverflows in /proc/net/netstat); alert on any non-zero rate over 1min.

bottlenecks.title: Consistent-hash stickiness hot-spotting on large multipart uploads
bottlenecks.trigger: Multipart uploads route all UploadPart calls to the same API replica via consistent-hash on upload_id. At 500K multipart completes/day with 5% being very large (5GB+), a single customer doing a 5TB upload pins 8-32 parallel streams to ONE API replica for minutes — while the LB thinks load is balanced.
bottlenecks.symptom: One API replica shows 95% CPU and elevated p99 latency on UploadPart while peers sit at 30%; LB metrics show even request distribution (because it IS distributing evenly by upload_id count, not by bytes).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use consistent-hash with bounded loads (Vimeo/Google algorithm): cap any backend at 1.25x mean load, overflow to next node in ring; alternatively hash on `(upload_id, part_number_range)` so parts of one upload spread across 2-4 replicas; store upload context in a shared cache (Redis) so stickiness is an optimization, not a requirement.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when any API replica's bytes/sec ingress exceeds 2x the fleet median for > 60s; track per-upload_id backend assignment cardinality and alert if p99 = 1 (all parts pinned) combined with upload size > 1GB.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a load balancer in front of the S3 API For an object storage service targeting **1M GETs/sec sustained and 3M at peak**, no single machine can terminate that many HTTPS connections, let alone process the requests. The API tier has to be a fleet — the design calls out ~2,000 API replicas across ~10 availability zones. Something has to stand in front of that fleet and decide which replica each request goes to. That's the load balancer's job here: it owns the public VIP (the address `s3.example.com` resolves to), terminates TLS once so the API replicas can talk plaintext inside the VPC (saving 3–5ms per request at a million requests/sec), and spreads connections across healthy replicas via least-connections. It also plays a subtler role for multipart uploads. When a client uploads a 5 GB object as 50 parts, those `UploadPart` calls benefit from landing on the same API replica that cached the upload context — so the LB consistent-hashes on `upload_id`. Without that stickiness, every part would trigger a fresh metadata lookup to reload the multipart state. ## What happens without it If clients hit API replicas directly, you lose health checking: a crashed or GC-paused replica keeps receiving traffic until DNS TTLs expire (minutes), and users see random 5xx errors. You also can't add or remove API replicas without clients noticing. ## The numbers At 3M peak GETs/sec across ~2,000 API replicas, each replica handles ~1,500 req/sec. The LB's job is keeping that distribution even — if one replica gets 5x the load because hashing is sloppy, it falls over at ~7,500 req/sec and the ejection logic (3 consecutive 5xx in 10s) has to kick in before clients notice. ## Trade-off The LB is now a failure domain of its own — hence the multi-AZ HA pair with anycast VIP, which adds operational complexity the API tier itself doesn't have.

api.name: S3 REST API
api.summary: Stateless service that speaks the S3 wire protocol: bucket ops, object PUT/GET/DELETE, multipart coordination, ACL.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
PUT /{bucket}/{key} # single-shot upload
GET /{bucket}/{key} # download
DELETE /{bucket}/{key} # tombstone
POST /{bucket}/{key}?uploads # InitiateMultipartUpload
PUT /{bucket}/{key}?partNumber=N&uploadId=U # UploadPart
POST /{bucket}/{key}?uploadId=U # CompleteMultipartUpload
```

sections.heading: PUT path
sections.body:
1. Auth (SigV4) → Auth Service
2. Allocate chunk placements from Metadata Service (returns list of data nodes)
3. Stream bytes to chosen data nodes via Replication Coordinator (erasure coding 6+3)
4. Wait for write quorum (at least 6 of 9 shards durably acked)
5. Commit metadata row (object → chunk list + version id)
6. Return ETag (MD5 of object or composite hash for multipart)

sections.heading: GET path
sections.body:
1. Auth
2. Lookup chunk placement in Metadata Service
3. Read enough shards to reconstruct (6 of 9 for EC) — parallel fan-out
4. If any shard errors, try the next data node holding a replica of that shard
5. Stream bytes back to client

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless → scale on CPU + network. At peak 3M GET QPS and ~10ms service time, ~2K replicas across ~10 AZs.

bottlenecks.title: Metadata service round-trips on the hot GET path
bottlenecks.trigger: Every GET at 1M sustained / 3M peak QPS requires a metadata lookup; with ~2000 API replicas that's ~500–1500 req/s/replica to metadata. Each lookup adds 3–10ms (meta service sim) on top of the API's own 5–20ms budget. At peak, a metadata slowdown from 5ms to 20ms blows the API's concurrency=3000 limit per replica (Little's law: 3000/0.04s = 75K/s capacity vs 3M/2000=1500/s required leaves little headroom if service time doubles).
bottlenecks.symptom: API replicas show rising p99 latency (>100ms) while CPU stays moderate; request queue depth climbs; 503s surface once per-replica in-flight requests exceed the concurrency cap. On-call sees correlated latency spikes between api and meta dashboards.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a near-cache on each API replica for (bucket,key,version) → chunk placements with 1–5s TTL, invalidated via the versioning log stream; this is safe because placements are immutable once written. Target >90% cache hit for hot keys. Also batch metadata lookups for multi-object ops (e.g., DeleteObjects) into a single RPC. Use gRPC connection pooling with HTTP/2 multiplexing to avoid TCP/TLS setup per lookup.
bottlenecks.detection: Track meta_lookup_latency_p99 per API replica and alert >15ms for 2min; track meta_cache_hit_ratio and alert <85%; track api_inflight_requests / concurrency_limit and alert >70%.

bottlenecks.title: Streaming memory pressure from large multipart UploadPart fan-in
bottlenecks.trigger: Capacity says ~5000 concurrent multipart uploads, each with 8–32 parallel part streams of 5–100MB. Per API replica (2000 replicas), that's ~2–16 concurrent UploadPart streams of up to 100MB each. If the API buffers any part of the stream before handing to the replication coordinator (for SigV4 chunk verification, MD5 compute, or EC encode pre-staging), memory per replica can spike to 100MB × 16 = 1.6GB just for in-flight PUT buffers, on top of GET streaming buffers.
bottlenecks.symptom: API replicas OOM-kill under sustained upload load, especially during backup windows (peak 300K PUT QPS); heap/RSS climbs proportional to concurrent multipart count; GC pauses (if JVM) cause correlated p99 GET latency spikes on the same replica.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Strict streaming pipeline: read from client socket directly into RS encoder with a bounded ring buffer (e.g., 8MB per stream), back-pressure the client TCP window rather than buffering. Cap per-replica concurrent multipart part streams (e.g., 32) and return 503 Slow Down above that, letting the LB shed to peers. Compute Content-MD5 incrementally during stream. Use x-amz-content-sha256=STREAMING-AWS4-HMAC-SHA256-PAYLOAD so signing doesn't require buffering.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on api_replica_rss > 75% of container limit; track api_inflight_upload_bytes gauge and alert when > 2GB/replica; monitor GC pause time p99 > 200ms; watch for 503 SlowDown rate climbing during backup windows.

bottlenecks.title: Replication coordinator tail latency poisoning PUT quorum waits
bottlenecks.trigger: PUT path waits for 6-of-9 EC shard acks with a 2s timeout (per repl design). At 100K sustained / 300K peak PUT QPS across 2000 API replicas = 50–150 in-flight PUTs per replica, each holding a request slot until quorum. Data node failureRate=0.001 and serviceTimeMs=[10,80] means ~0.1% of shard writes go slow or fail; with 9 shards per chunk the probability of at least one slow shard per PUT is ~1 - 0.999^9 ≈ 0.9%, pushing PUT tail toward the slowest-of-6 order statistic.
bottlenecks.symptom: PUT p99 latency rises to hundreds of ms during partial data-node degradation; API concurrency=3000 slots fill with stuck PUTs waiting for quorum; cascades to 503s on new requests including GETs on the same replica; multipart completes stall because individual UploadParts time out.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Hedge the 7th–9th shard writes: if the 5th ack arrives, start a hedged write to a backup placement for the slowest in-flight shard. Lower the quorum timeout to 500ms and fail fast (client retry is cheap, holding a slot isn't). Isolate PUT and GET thread pools / concurrency budgets per replica so PUT stalls can't starve GETs. Use data-node health signal from placement service to avoid known-slow nodes.
bottlenecks.detection: Track put_quorum_wait_ms_p99 and alert >300ms; track shard_write_slowest_p99 vs p50 ratio and alert >5x; monitor api_replica_inflight_puts / total_inflight and alert when PUTs consume >60% of concurrency budget.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the S3 REST API tier is here For an S3-like service, clients speak a very specific wire protocol: SigV4-signed HTTPS, multipart upload semantics, ETag/version-id headers, XML error bodies. Something has to *be* that protocol — parse the request, authenticate it, figure out where the bytes should live, orchestrate the erasure-coded write across 9 data nodes, and stitch the response back together. The API tier is that translator. It's deliberately **stateless** so you can scale it horizontally on CPU and network, because neither the metadata service (strongly-consistent, expensive to scale) nor the data nodes (pinned to their disks) can absorb a million signed HTTPS requests per second on their own. ## What happens without it If clients talked directly to data nodes, every SDK would need to know the EC scheme, the placement algorithm, shard-level retries, and how to do a quorum write — and a buggy client could corrupt data or DoS a data node by picking bad placements. Metadata lookups would also fan out from the client, multiplying round-trips across the internet. The API tier absorbs that orchestration so data nodes stay "dumb" and metadata stays small. ## The numbers At peak 3M GET QPS with ~10ms service time, Little's Law says we need ~30,000 concurrent request slots. At a concurrency cap of ~3,000 per replica (sim), that's **~10 replicas minimum just for peak GETs** — the design provisions ~2,000 across 10 AZs for headroom, failure domains, and PUT orchestration (which is heavier). ## Trade-off An extra network hop (client → API → data node) adds latency, but you gain a single place to enforce auth, versioning, and EC invariants.

auth.name: Auth Service
auth.summary: Validates SigV4 signatures, enforces bucket policies and IAM ACLs.

sections.heading: Signing
sections.body:
```
# SigV4 validation (simplified)
canonical = method + '\n' + path + '\n' + canonical_query(...)
string_to_sign = 'AWS4-HMAC-SHA256\n' + timestamp + '\n' + credential_scope + '\n' + sha256(canonical)
kSigning = derive_key(secret, date, region, 's3')
expected = hmac_sha256(kSigning, string_to_sign)
assert expected == req.headers['X-Amz-Signature']
```

sections.heading: Policy evaluation
sections.body: Combined decision from bucket policy, IAM policy, and object ACL. Explicit Deny > Explicit Allow > Implicit Deny. Policies are cached on the auth replica (LRU, 60s TTL) to avoid a per-request DB lookup.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: Auth is on the critical path. Local policy cache + secret-key cache means we tolerate brief policy-DB outages — but a cold auth replica sees ~10ms of extra latency on first request per bucket.

bottlenecks.title: SigV4 HMAC-SHA256 CPU saturation at peak fan-in
bottlenecks.trigger: Every request (PUT + GET + UploadPart) hits auth before any data path work. At peak 3M GET + 300K PUT QPS = ~3.3M SigV4 verifications/sec. Each verification is ~4 HMAC-SHA256 rounds over the canonical request (~5-50 KB of canonical string for large headers), costing ~50-200 µs of CPU. At concurrency=5000 per replica and serviceTimeMs=[3,10], a replica sustains ~500-1500 req/sec — needing 2000-6000 auth replicas just for signature math.
bottlenecks.symptom: Auth replicas pin at 95%+ CPU while policy-DB and network sit idle; p99 authz latency climbs from 10ms to 100ms+; API tier observes stuck inflight requests waiting on auth; 503s surface uniformly across all operations (both GETs and PUTs degrade together, which is the giveaway vs. a data-path issue).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Offload HMAC to AES-NI / SHA-NI accelerated libraries (OpenSSL 3.x with EVP_MAC, BoringSSL); cache derived signing keys per (access_key, date, region, service) with 24h TTL — the kSigning key is reusable across all requests from the same caller that day, eliminating 3 of the 4 HMAC rounds; pool goroutines/threads to NUMA-pin crypto work; autoscale auth replicas on CPU utilization (target 60%) not QPS.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on auth_replica_cpu_pct > 70% sustained 5min; track sigv4_verify_latency_p99 > 20ms; monitor signing_key_cache_hit_ratio and alert when < 95% (indicates cache thrashing or under-sized LRU); watch hmac_ops_per_sec per replica against the known CPU budget.

bottlenecks.title: Policy cache cold-start and invalidation storms
bottlenecks.trigger: Policy cache has LRU 60s TTL per auth replica. With ~2000-6000 auth replicas and policies spread across millions of buckets, every TTL expiry forces a policy-DB lookup adding ~10ms. If a large tenant (e.g., analytics fleet hitting one bucket at 100K GETs/sec) has its policy TTL expire simultaneously across all replicas, that's a 100K/sec thundering herd on the policy DB. Cold auth replica spinning up during autoscale sees 100% miss for the first ~60s of traffic.
bottlenecks.symptom: Periodic 60s-cadence latency spikes on GET/PUT p99 correlated across the fleet; policy-DB connection pool exhaustion; new auth replicas report elevated first-request latency; bucket-policy UPDATE operations cause brief error bursts as caches invalidate non-atomically across replicas.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use randomized TTL jitter (60s ± 15s) to de-synchronize expiries; add request-coalescing (singleflight pattern) so concurrent misses for the same (principal, bucket) trigger one DB lookup; implement negative caching for Deny decisions with shorter TTL (10s) to bound staleness on revocation; use a two-tier cache (per-replica L1 + shared Redis L2) so cold replicas warm in <1s; push policy updates via pub/sub (on the versioning log or a dedicated channel) for coherent invalidation rather than pure TTL.
bottlenecks.detection: Track policy_cache_hit_ratio per replica and alert < 98%; alert on policy_db_qps > 10K (indicates herd); monitor p99 sigv4_policy_eval_latency and alert on periodic spikes (FFT or autocorrelation on 60s period); track policy_update_propagation_lag_ms.

bottlenecks.title: Clock skew rejecting valid SigV4 requests under the 15-minute window
bottlenecks.trigger: SigV4 mandates the request timestamp (x-amz-date) be within ±15 min of server time, else reject with RequestTimeTooSkewed. Across ~2000-6000 auth replicas spanning 10 AZs, NTP drift or a misconfigured replica can silently push one replica's clock outside the window. At 3.3M QPS, even a 0.1% of auth traffic landing on a skewed replica = 3300 false rejections/sec; clients that don't rotate through SDK retries hit hard 403s.
bottlenecks.symptom: A subset of clients see sporadic 403 RequestTimeTooSkewed errors that clear on retry (because the LB picks a different auth replica); support tickets about 'intermittent auth failures' that can't be reproduced; metrics show 403 rate concentrated on specific auth replica IDs rather than uniform.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run chrony with multiple stratum-1 NTP sources (PTP where available) and alert if offset > 100ms; health-check auth replicas by injecting a synthetic SigV4 request with a known-good timestamp and eject replicas returning skew errors; tighten internal monitoring to ±1s while keeping the external contract at ±15min; use TAI or a leader-provided timestamp for logging to make skew detectable in audit.
bottlenecks.detection: Export node_time_offset_seconds per replica and alert > 1s; track sigv4_skew_rejection_rate per replica_id and alert when any single replica's rate is > 3 stddev above fleet median; correlate 403 RequestTimeTooSkewed spikes against replica rollouts.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a dedicated Auth Service in an S3-like system For an object storage service holding exabytes of customer data across millions of buckets, **every single request** — PUT, GET, DELETE, every UploadPart — has to prove who the caller is and whether their IAM policy + bucket policy allows the operation. You can't bolt this onto the API tier as a library call, because the policy evaluation itself is non-trivial (combining bucket policy, IAM policy, and object ACL with "explicit Deny beats Allow" semantics), and the signing-key derivation for SigV4 is CPU-heavy enough that you want to scale and cache it independently from the request-handling fleet. Pulling it into its own service lets you scale crypto-bound work separately from the I/O-bound API tier, and centralizes the policy cache so one bucket-policy change propagates predictably. ## What happens without it If auth lived inside each API replica as inline code, a cold API replica on deploy would hit the policy database for every new bucket it saw — a million-QPS fleet would hammer the policy DB into the ground. Worse, a signing bug or a leaked credential couldn't be revoked centrally; you'd be chasing config across ~2,000 API replicas. Users would see sporadic 403s during deploys, and operators would see policy-DB latency spikes correlated with API autoscaling events. ## The numbers At **1M sustained GETs/sec plus 100K PUTs/sec**, that's ~1.1M SigV4 verifications per second. Each verification is 4 HMAC-SHA256 rounds (~50–200µs CPU). Caching the derived signing key per `(access_key, date)` collapses 3 of those 4 rounds — so the cache alone saves roughly 1.1M × 150µs × 3 = **~500 CPU-seconds per wall-clock second**, or ~500 cores of work. That's the difference between needing 2,000 auth replicas and needing 6,000. ## Trade-off Auth is now on the critical path of every request — one extra hop of latency (~3–10ms) and a new failure domain — but the operator gets one place to rotate keys, audit denials, and cache policy decisions coherently.

meta.name: Metadata Service (Index)
meta.summary: Strongly-consistent index mapping (bucket, key, version) → chunk placements + object attributes.

sections.heading: Schema
sections.body:
```
TABLE objects bucket TEXT key TEXT version_id UUID size_bytes BIGINT content_type TEXT etag TEXT chunks JSONB -- [{chunk_id, size, shards:[{node_id, disk, shard_idx}]}] created_at TIMESTAMP tombstone BOOL PRIMARY KEY ((bucket, key), version_id DESC)
```

sections.heading: Why a sharded SQL (Spanner / CockroachDB)
sections.body: Two hard requirements: (a) strong consistency on version order (reads must see the latest write), (b) efficient range scans for ListObjects. Both are awkward in a pure KV store. Shard by hash(bucket, key) — uniform load, no hot partitions as long as keys are well-distributed.

sections.heading: Chunk placement policy
sections.body: New chunk → placement service picks 9 data nodes spread across 3 AZs (3 per AZ) to maximize fault isolation. Placement is cached in the returned metadata row.

sections.heading: Consistency
sections.body: Read-after-write for PUT → GET on the same key (S3 has offered this since 2020). Implemented via linearizable reads from the shard leader; serializable for multi-key list ops.

lost: No server-side range scan with ordering
Eventual consistency breaks strong PUT→GET contract without QUORUM-everywhere

bottlenecks.title: Hot shard from single-bucket key prefix concentration
bottlenecks.trigger: Metadata is sharded by hash(bucket, key) across ~10K nodes, so each shard handles ~110 QPS average of the 1.1M total (1M GET + 100K PUT lookups). But a single large-tenant bucket with a timestamp-prefixed key pattern (e.g., logs/2026-04-24/...) during ML training at 100K-300K GET/sec on one bucket lands 10-100x the mean on the shards owning that bucket's key range. With concurrency=3000 per shard and serviceTimeMs=[3,10], a shard saturates at ~300-1000 QPS.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 metadata lookup latency on affected shards jumps from ~8ms to 100ms+ while cluster-wide p50 stays flat; API tier shows correlated GET latency spikes only for specific buckets; Spanner/Cockroach leader CPU at 95% on 2-3 shards while peers sit at 20%.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Add a per-API-replica read-through cache keyed on (bucket, key, version_id) → chunks with 1-5s TTL (safe because chunk placements are immutable once written, invalidation via versioning log tail); shard on hash(bucket, key_prefix_bucket) where prefix_bucket = first 2 bytes of SHA256(key) to spread hot prefixes; use CockroachDB's load-based splitting to auto-split hot ranges at >250 QPS per range.
bottlenecks.detection: Export per-shard QPS and p99 latency; alert when any shard's QPS > 5x fleet median for >60s, or when shard p99 latency > 30ms; track range-split events per hour as a leading indicator of hot-spotting.

bottlenecks.title: Multi-row commit contention on CompleteMultipartUpload
bottlenecks.trigger: CompleteMultipartUpload runs a transaction that SELECTs all part rows, INSERTs the object version, and DELETEs the pending multipart rows — across potentially different shards (parts keyed by upload_id, object row keyed by bucket+key). At 500K multipart completes/day peak-loaded into ~8 hours of backup windows = ~17 completes/sec average but ~100/sec at peak, each touching 10-1000 part rows. Cross-shard 2PC in Spanner/Cockroach costs 2-3x a single-shard write and holds locks on pending_multipart rows that concurrent UploadParts may contend on.
bottlenecks.symptom: Complete operations see p99 latency spikes to 500ms+ during backup windows; retry-induced duplicate Complete attempts cause 'transaction aborted: retry' errors in logs; pending_multipart table grows because cleanup DELETEs fail mid-transaction; API tier holds request slots waiting on Complete, starving other PUTs.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Co-locate multipart_parts rows with the object row by sharding parts on hash(bucket, key) instead of upload_id (keeps the transaction single-shard); use Spanner interleaved tables / Cockroach INTERLEAVE IN PARENT; move the DELETE of part rows out of the commit transaction into an async cleanup driven by versioning log (commit only writes the object row + a 'complete' marker); cap per-object part count at 10,000 (S3 standard) to bound transaction size.
bottlenecks.detection: Track complete_multipart_txn_latency_p99 > 200ms; alert on txn_retry_rate > 1% for Complete ops; monitor pending_multipart_rows growth rate — steady-state should be zero net growth, alert on >5% daily increase; track cross-shard vs single-shard txn ratio.

bottlenecks.title: ListObjects range scans blocking leader on deep buckets
bottlenecks.trigger: ListObjects is served as a range scan on the primary key ((bucket, key), version_id DESC). A bucket with 100M+ objects (large tenants easily hit this with 10T total / ~millions of buckets) issuing a paginated LIST at 1000 keys/page requires scanning through tombstones + non-current versions, which can mean reading 10K+ rows to produce 1K results. At linearizable read consistency from the shard leader, each LIST pins a leader read slot for 50-500ms.
bottlenecks.symptom: LIST p99 latency in the seconds for deep buckets; correlated GET latency increase on the same shard because leader read queue backs up; clients time out and retry, amplifying load; shard CPU dominated by scan work rather than point lookups.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Serve LIST from follower reads with bounded staleness (Spanner stale reads at 10s, Cockroach AS OF SYSTEM TIME) — LIST doesn't need linearizability; add a secondary index on (bucket, key) WHERE tombstone=false AND is_current_version=true to skip tombstones and old versions at scan time; enforce MaxKeys ≤ 1000 and require ContinuationToken for deeper pagination; cache common prefix listings in API-tier for 1-5s.
bottlenecks.detection: Track list_latency_p99 per bucket and alert > 1s; monitor rows_scanned / rows_returned ratio per LIST op, alert when > 10x (indicates tombstone bloat); alert on leader_read_queue_depth > 100 on any shard; track LIST QPS as fraction of total meta QPS.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a separate Metadata Service exists here For an S3-like store holding **10 trillion objects** spread across **300,000 data nodes**, the fundamental question on every request is: *"where do the bytes for `my-bucket/datasets/2026-q1.parquet` actually live?"* Data nodes are dumb — they know about shard files on their local disks, not about buckets, keys, or versions. Something has to own the mapping from `(bucket, key, version)` → `[9 shard locations across 3 AZs]`, and it has to be **strongly consistent** so that a GET issued 1ms after a successful PUT sees the new version (S3's read-after-write guarantee since 2020). That's what the metadata service is: a small, sharded, SQL-like index that's the source of truth for placement and versioning. ## What happens without it If you baked placement into a hash function instead (like Ceph's CRUSH), you'd lose versioning and tombstoning — two features S3 users rely on — and every rebalance would require rewriting data. If you stored metadata inline with the data nodes, a ListObjects on a bucket with 100M keys would have to fan out to thousands of nodes. Users would see inconsistent listings, stale reads after PUT, and DELETE operations that flicker back to life. ## The numbers **10 trillion objects × ~1 KB of metadata each = 10 PB of index**, sharded across ~10K metadata nodes (so ~1 TB each — comfortable for SSD). At 1M GETs/sec, that's ~100 lookups/sec per shard on average — trivial for a SQL shard, which is exactly why separating it from the 200 GB/s data plane works. ## Trade-off Every request now pays one extra metadata round-trip (~3–10ms) before any byte moves — the price of having a coherent, queryable index over exabytes of otherwise opaque blobs.

data.name: Data Node
data.summary: Storage server holding on-disk shards; exposes chunk-level PUT/GET via an internal RPC.

sections.heading: Layout
sections.body:
Each node owns 10–30 disks (HDD for cold tier, NVMe for hot). Shards laid out on disk as append-only log files with a local index:
```
/disk-03/ext_19821/shard_7c11_2.dat # chunk_id 7c11..., shard_idx 2
/disk-03/ext_19821/shard_7c11_2.idx # offset table
```

sections.heading: Durability on disk
sections.body:
- fsync before ack (tunable; hot tier uses battery-backed RAID controllers to batch)
- Background scrubber reads + CRC-checks all shards weekly; rebuild from EC parity on bit-rot
- Fail-in-place: bad disks removed from rotation, replicator rebuilds affected shards to peers

sections.heading: Throughput
sections.body: Single node: ~2 GB/s read, ~500 MB/s write on NVMe tier. Fleet: 300K nodes → hundreds of TB/s aggregate. GET path dominated by network to client, not disk.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: Node down → replication coordinator re-issues failed shard writes to a peer in the same AZ. Permanent node loss → background re-replication job rebuilds all shards from the remaining 6 of 9 in the EC stripe.

gained: Simpler recovery (just copy one surviving replica)
Lower GET tail latency — no reconstruction math

lost: 16 shards per chunk spreads more — rebuild reads 12 peers for any one loss

bottlenecks.title: Disk I/O saturation on EC shard fan-in/fan-out
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1M GET QPS × 200KB avg = 200 GB/s read egress, each GET fans out 6 shard reads across the 300K-node fleet; that's ~6M shard reads/sec, ~20 shard reads/sec/node. PUTs add 300K/sec × 9 shards = 2.7M shard writes/sec. A single node with 10-30 HDDs at ~150 IOPS each (~3000 IOPS total) saturates once small-object traffic concentrates — hot extents on HDD tier can't absorb >500 MB/s sustained or random small reads at scale.
bottlenecks.symptom: p99 shard read latency climbs from ~3ms (page cache) to 40-200ms (HDD seek); repl coordinator sees slow-shard timeouts and triggers EC reconstruction more often, which reads 6 shards from peers and amplifies load; GET tail latency spikes on hot buckets while fleet-wide CPU looks idle.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Tier hot data on NVMe (2 GB/s/node) and cold on HDD with explicit placement hints in metadata; use log-structured append-only extents (already in design) to turn random writes into sequential; add an in-memory LRU for small-object shards (<64KB) sized to ~10% of RAM per node; throttle background scrubber + GC quarantine releases to <10% disk I/O budget.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-disk util% > 80% sustained 60s; shard_read_latency_p99 > 50ms on NVMe or > 200ms on HDD; ratio of ec_reconstruct_reads / total_gets > 1% (indicates slow-shard fallback firing); alert on page_cache_hit_ratio < 70% for hot tier.

bottlenecks.title: Rebuild storm on permanent node loss
bottlenecks.trigger: With 300K nodes at 10TB each and ~1% annual failure rate, ~8 nodes/day fail permanently. Each lost node holds ~10TB of shards spread across ~1M chunks; rebuilding requires reading 6 peer shards per chunk to reconstruct the lost one = 60TB of peer read traffic per failed node. If 3 nodes fail in the same AZ within the rebuild window (hours), the EC 6+3 stripe is one shard from data loss.
bottlenecks.symptom: Cross-node replication bandwidth spikes to 10s of GB/s within an AZ; peer data nodes serving rebuild reads show elevated p99 GET latency for user traffic; on-call sees 'shard under-replicated' alerts compounding if rebuild can't keep up with failure rate; durability budget (11 nines) degrades during correlated failures.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Prioritized rebuild queue: chunks with only 6 surviving shards rebuild before those with 7+; cap rebuild bandwidth at 25% of node NIC (e.g., 2.5 GB/s of a 10 GbE link) to protect user traffic; spread replacement shards across multiple target nodes rather than one, parallelizing the rebuild; use copysets to limit the number of chunks affected by any given 3-node correlated failure.
bottlenecks.detection: Track under_replicated_chunks by surviving_shard_count bucket; alert when any chunk has <7 surviving shards for >10min; monitor rebuild_bandwidth_gbps vs rebuild_backlog_bytes — alert if backlog grows for >30min; durability SLO burn-rate alert on estimated_annual_loss_probability.

bottlenecks.title: Silent bit-rot outpacing scrubber cycle
bottlenecks.trigger: 3 EB raw across 300K nodes at ~10TB each. HDD unrecoverable bit-error rate is ~1 per 10^14 bits read = ~1 per 12.5TB; across 3EB that's ~240K latent corruptions at any time. Weekly scrubber must read all 3EB/week = ~5 TB/s fleet-wide scrub bandwidth (~17 MB/s/node) — eats into user I/O budget, and any scrubber slowdown means corruptions accumulate faster than detection.
bottlenecks.symptom: GET returns CRC32C mismatch on shard read, triggering EC reconstruction transparently — but if correlated corruption hits 4+ shards of the same stripe (e.g., firmware bug across a disk batch) the chunk is unrecoverable and surfaces as a 500 to the client; scrubber falls behind its weekly SLA and bit_rot_detected rate rises.
bottlenecks.mitigation: CRC32C on every shard read path (already in design) + background scrubber with adaptive rate (faster during low user traffic); shard across disk vendors/firmware within an EC stripe to avoid correlated failure batches; add end-to-end checksum stored in metadata so post-reconstruction bytes are verified before returning to client; pre-emptively scrub disks showing rising SMART reallocated-sector counts.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on scrubber_cycle_days > 10 (SLA is 7); crc_mismatch_rate per node — outliers >3 stddev indicate a failing disk; track ec_reconstruct_due_to_crc / ec_reconstruct_due_to_timeout ratio; SMART attribute monitoring for Reallocated_Sector_Ct and Current_Pending_Sector.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Data Nodes are here For an S3-like service storing **3 exabytes of raw bytes**, something has to physically hold those bytes on spinning disks and SSDs. That's all a data node is: a server with 10–30 disks attached, exposing a dumb "write this shard, read that shard" RPC. The design deliberately keeps them *dumb* — they don't know about buckets, keys, versions, or users. That knowledge lives in the metadata service. Data nodes just store opaque shard files and verify checksums. This separation is what makes the system scale: you can add 10,000 data nodes next quarter without touching the metadata layer at all. ## What happens without them If you tried to store objects directly in the metadata database, a single 5 GB video upload would blow up the SQL shard's write-ahead log, and serving 200 GB/s of read egress from a query engine would be laughable — SQL engines aren't built to stream gigabytes. You'd also lose erasure coding: the whole point of splitting a chunk into 9 shards across 3 AZs is that independent storage nodes can fail independently. Without that isolation, one rack fire loses a customer's data. ## The numbers The design targets **200 GB/s of read egress** across the fleet. A single data node sustains ~2 GB/s on the NVMe hot tier, so you need roughly 200 / 2 = **100 data nodes actively serving** at any moment just for peak reads — and the fleet is sized at **300,000 nodes** (3 EB ÷ 10 TB/node) for capacity, giving enormous headroom for failure domains and cold storage. ## Trade-off Keeping data nodes dumb means every request pays an extra network hop through the API tier, but it buys independent scaling of storage and compute.

repl.name: Replication Coordinator
repl.summary: Drives the erasure-coded write: encodes chunks into 6+3 shards and fans them out to data nodes.

sections.heading: Reed-Solomon 6+3
sections.body: Chunk is split into 6 data shards; 3 parity shards computed via Reed-Solomon over GF(2^8). Any 6 of the 9 shards reconstruct the original — tolerates 3 simultaneous shard losses. Overhead: 9/6 = 1.5x vs 3x for full replication.

sections.heading: Write quorum
sections.body:
```
shards = rs_encode(chunk_bytes, k=6, m=3) # 9 shards
fanout: for i, shard in enumerate(shards): async data_nodes[i].put(chunk_id, i, shard)
wait until >= 6 acks within 2s
if acks < 6: abort write, surface 503
```
Write quorum of 6 guarantees every shard is on at least one live node at commit time; the remaining 3 parity shards are repaired asynchronously if any failed.

sections.heading: Read degraded mode
sections.body: If a shard read times out, fetch any other shard; with 9 shards and k=6 needed, one slow node is invisible. With 3 slow nodes we reconstruct from the 6 fastest and pay the RS-decode CPU cost (~2–10ms per MB).

sections.heading: Parallel fanout
sections.body: All 9 PUTs issued in parallel — end-to-end PUT latency is the p50 of the 6th-fastest shard, not the slowest. In practice this pulls p99 PUT down 2–3x vs serial writes.

bottlenecks.title: Tail-latency amplification from slowest-of-6 shard writes
bottlenecks.trigger: PUT quorum requires 6-of-9 shard acks with a 2s timeout. At 100K sustained / 300K peak PUT QPS, each PUT fans out 9 parallel writes to data nodes with serviceTimeMs=[10,80] and failureRate=0.001. Probability at least one of 9 shards is slow (>p99) is 1-(0.99)^9 ≈ 8.6%, and for the 6th-fastest the order statistic pulls PUT p99 toward the slow tail of the data-node distribution.
bottlenecks.symptom: PUT p99 latency climbs from ~60ms (expected 6th-order of 9 samples from [15,60]) to 500ms+ during partial data-node degradation; coordinator concurrency=2000 slots fill with PUTs waiting for the 6th ack; 503 WriteQuorumNotMet errors surface under correlated slowness; API replicas back up waiting on repl.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Hedge writes: as soon as 5 acks arrive, start backup writes for the 2 slowest in-flight shards to alternative placements. Shorten quorum timeout from 2s to 500ms (client retry is cheaper than holding a slot). Use health-aware placement from the placement service to avoid known-slow nodes proactively. Track p99 per-node write latency as placement input.
bottlenecks.detection: Track repl_put_quorum_wait_ms_p99 and alert >200ms; track slow_shard_fraction (shards >p95 of fleet) per PUT and alert >5%; alert when write_quorum_not_met_rate > 0.1% over 1min; monitor 6th-ack-vs-fastest-ack latency ratio and alert when > 10x.

bottlenecks.title: RS encode/decode CPU saturation at peak throughput
bottlenecks.trigger: Every PUT runs rs_encode(k=6,m=3) over the chunk; every GET with any slow/failed shard runs rs_decode. At 100K PUT QPS × 200KB avg = 20 GB/s of encoding; peak 300K × 200KB = 60 GB/s. RS over GF(2^8) costs ~2-10ms CPU per MB without SIMD (serviceTimeMs=[15,60] sim includes this). Additionally, ~1% of GETs (data node failureRate=0.001 × 9 shards) trigger decode, adding 10-30 GB/s decode work at peak 3M GET QPS.
bottlenecks.symptom: Coordinator replicas pin at 95%+ CPU during backup windows; encode_latency_p99 climbs from 18ms (sim baseline) to 100ms+; PUT concurrency=2000 budget fills with encode-bound requests; GET p99 spikes only for objects requiring reconstruction, while happy-path GETs stay flat — classic asymmetric degradation that's hard to diagnose.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use ISA-L (Intel Storage Acceleration Library) or Jerasure with AVX2/AVX-512 SIMD — 10-30x faster than scalar GF(2^8). Offload to dedicated encode/decode worker pools pinned to NUMA nodes. Consider hardware offload (Intel QAT) for high-volume regions. Scale repl replicas on CPU (target 60%) not QPS, since object size skew causes high variance.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on repl_cpu_pct > 70% sustained 5min; track encode_mb_per_cpu_sec and alert when < 500 MB/s/core (indicates SIMD not engaged); track decode_invocation_rate / get_rate and alert > 2% (indicates upstream data-node health issue driving decode load); monitor p99 encode_latency_ms per chunk-size bucket.

bottlenecks.title: Coordinator as single-write-path failure domain for all PUTs
bottlenecks.trigger: Every PUT (100K sustained, 300K peak) flows through repl — it holds the in-flight chunk bytes, orchestrates 9 fanout RPCs, and gates the commit. With concurrency=2000 per replica and serviceTimeMs=[15,60] (p50 ~30ms), per-replica capacity is ~60K QPS — so only ~5 replicas needed for peak, a small fleet. Any repl replica crash drops up to 2000 in-flight PUTs that must be restarted by clients; correlated crashes (bad deploy, memory bug in RS lib) can take down the write plane while GETs continue serving.
bottlenecks.symptom: PUT availability SLO (99.9%) burns rapidly during repl incidents while GET availability (99.99%) stays green — asymmetric outage confuses on-call. Clients see bursts of 503 with no corresponding data-node or metadata errors. In-flight multipart UploadParts fail, forcing SDK restarts of entire parts (50-100MB re-upload).
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run repl as ≥20 replicas across 3 AZs even though capacity math says 5 — headroom for correlated failures and rolling deploys. Make the coordinator stateless: stream bytes through without buffering the full chunk (ring buffer to RS encoder), so a crash loses one request not 2000. Implement idempotent PUT via client-provided chunk_id so retries don't create orphan shards. Canary deploys with 5% traffic + automatic rollback on 503 rate > 0.5%.
bottlenecks.detection: Track repl_replica_count vs min_required_for_peak and alert when ratio < 3x; alert on put_503_rate > 0.1% over 1min; monitor in_flight_puts_per_replica and alert > 80% of concurrency cap; track orphan_shard_rate (shards written but no metadata commit) as a canary for repl crashes mid-write.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Replication Coordinator exists here For an S3-like service promising **11 nines of durability** across exabytes of data, every PUT has to land on disk in a way that survives independent failures of disks, nodes, racks, and whole availability zones. The design chose Reed-Solomon 6+3 erasure coding over 3x replication — it cuts storage overhead from 3x to 1.5x, which at 3 EB of raw data saves you roughly 4.5 EB of disk. But EC is *not* a client-friendly primitive: you can't just "write one copy." Every chunk has to be split into 6 data shards, have 3 parity shards computed over a Galois field, and be fanned out to 9 different data nodes spread across 3 AZs — then you have to wait for a write quorum before committing. The coordinator is the specialist that owns that orchestration so the API tier doesn't have to. ## What happens without it If the API tier did this inline, every API replica would need the RS codec, placement-aware retry logic, and hedging for slow shards. A bug in any of that corrupts data silently. Worse, without a dedicated quorum-waiter, one slow disk on one data node stalls the whole PUT — users see p99 latencies in seconds, and operators see API threads pinned waiting on the single stuck shard. ## The numbers At **100K sustained PUTs/sec**, each PUT fans out to 9 data nodes, so the coordinator fleet drives **900K shard writes/sec**. Waiting for 6-of-9 acks (not 9-of-9) means the p99 PUT tracks the *6th-fastest* shard out of 9 — if each shard has a 1% chance of being slow, the chance that at least 4 of 9 are slow (blocking quorum) is under 0.001%, versus 9% for a 9-of-9 scheme. That's the whole game. ## Trade-off You accept a heavier write path (RS encode + 9 RPCs per chunk) in exchange for halving your storage bill and shrinking tail latency via over-provisioned parallelism.

vlog.name: Versioning Log
vlog.summary: Append-only log of every metadata mutation (PUT version, DELETE tombstone, LifecycleExpire).

sections.heading: Shape
sections.body: `(timestamp, bucket, key, version_id, op, actor)` — op ∈ {PUT, DELETE, RESTORE, LIFECYCLE_EXPIRE}. Partitioned by hash(bucket, key) across Kafka topics.

sections.heading: Consumers
sections.body:
- GC worker: reads tombstones, schedules chunk deletion after 7d grace
- Replication to other regions (cross-region replication feature)
- Audit / CloudTrail-style logging
- Billing: size deltas per bucket per hour

sections.heading: Retention
sections.body: 30d hot in Kafka, archived to S3 itself (dogfood) for compliance. Version history on an object is derived from this log plus the metadata table.

bottlenecks.title: Write fan-in from every metadata mutation saturates partition leaders
bottlenecks.trigger: Every PUT, DELETE, lifecycle expire, and multipart complete emits a CDC event. At 100K sustained PUTs/sec + ~10K DELETEs/sec + 500K/day multipart completes + background LIFECYCLE_EXPIRE sweeps on 10T objects, steady-state write rate is ~110K events/sec with peaks to ~320K/sec during backup windows. Partitioned by hash(bucket, key); a Kafka topic with 100 partitions means ~3.2K events/sec/partition peak, but a whale bucket with 30% of traffic lands 100K events/sec on a handful of partition leaders — well past the ~50K msg/sec/partition sustainable ceiling with fsync-on-ack.
bottlenecks.symptom: Producer-side latency spikes (p99 append >100ms) on meta service commits because the CDC emit is on the commit path; hot partition leaders show 95%+ disk util while peer partitions idle; downstream GC/billing consumers lag by minutes; correlated PUT p99 latency increase in the metadata tier because the versioning-log emit blocks the commit.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Over-partition aggressively (e.g., 1000 partitions) and hash on (bucket, key, hour_bucket) to smear whale buckets across partitions at the cost of out-of-order-within-bucket (consumers already idempotent on version_id); make the CDC emit async-after-commit using an outbox pattern in the metadata SQL so meta commits don't block on Kafka; tune Kafka producer with acks=1+min.insync.replicas=2, linger.ms=5, batch.size=256KB, compression=zstd to push per-partition throughput to ~200K msg/sec; autoscale partition count using Confluent Elastic or manual repartition on sustained lag.
bottlenecks.detection: Per-partition produce rate histogram — alert when any partition exceeds 3x fleet median for >60s; kafka_log_append_latency_p99 per broker >50ms; meta_commit_to_vlog_emit_latency_ms_p99 >20ms (indicates emit on critical path); UnderReplicatedPartitions >0 on any broker.

bottlenecks.title: Consumer lag on GC unbounded-grows reclaimable storage debt
bottlenecks.trigger: GC consumes the DELETE/LIFECYCLE_EXPIRE stream to schedule shard quarantine 7 days after delete. With ~10K DELETEs/sec + lifecycle expiries on 10T objects (even 0.01%/day lifecycle hits = 1B events/day = ~12K/sec), GC must sustain ~25K events/sec; each event fans out to 9 quarantine RPCs across data nodes = 225K RPCs/sec. GC is throttled to 10% disk I/O per design, so any sustained incoming-event rate above GC's effective rate causes the log backlog to grow unboundedly — and reclaimable-but-not-reclaimed bytes accumulate on the 3EB fleet.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka consumer lag on the gc consumer group climbs from seconds to hours to days; disk-free metrics on data nodes plateau or shrink despite user DELETEs; on-call sees 'reclaimable_bytes' gauge diverging from 'reclaimed_bytes'; cluster starts rejecting PUTs with 507 InsufficientStorage even though logical free space exists; 30-day Kafka retention risks rolling off un-processed DELETE events = silent storage leak.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Parallelize GC consumers per partition with at-least-once semantics and idempotent quarantine (keyed on chunk_id+shard_idx); scale GC worker count to match partition count so per-partition lag stays <60s; add a priority lane in GC for events older than 5 days (approaching Kafka retention); back-pressure the log by extending retention to 90d for DELETE topic specifically; emit a 'gc_backlog_bytes_equivalent' metric from consumer lag × avg object size to quantify storage debt.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka consumer_group_lag for 'gc' >10M messages or >1h time-lag; alert when reclaimable_bytes - reclaimed_bytes trends positive over 24h window; alert if any DELETE event is <7d from Kafka retention cutoff AND not yet processed (imminent data-leak bug); track gc_events_consumed_per_sec vs log_events_produced_per_sec ratio and alert <0.95 sustained.

bottlenecks.title: Retention + fanout multiplies log storage into petabytes
bottlenecks.trigger: 30-day hot retention in Kafka across ~110K events/sec avg × ~500 bytes/event (with bucket/key/version_id/actor) = ~4.8 TB/day raw, ×30d = ~140 TB hot; with 3x Kafka replication = ~420 TB resident on Kafka brokers. Additionally 4 consumer groups (GC, cross-region repl, audit, billing) each maintain independent offsets and may fan-out re-reads during replay/recovery, multiplying broker read I/O by 4x. Cross-region replication further duplicates the full stream to remote regions.
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka broker disk fills faster than capacity planning assumed; broker page-cache hit rate drops as working set exceeds RAM, pushing tail reads to disk and elevating consumer read latency; cross-region replication bandwidth saturates inter-region links during replay; archival-to-S3 job can't keep up, forcing retention reduction which breaks 30-day compliance.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Kafka tiered storage (Confluent Tiered Storage or KIP-405) to offload segments >24h old to S3 (dogfood) while keeping metadata on brokers — cuts broker disk from 420TB to ~20TB; compress events with zstd level 3 (~3-5x on JSON events) → ~100TB effective; schema-encode events with Avro/Protobuf instead of JSON (another 2-3x reduction); shard audit/billing consumers to read only their needed fields via a projection layer; rate-limit cross-region replication to off-peak.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on kafka broker disk_used_pct >70%; track bytes_in_per_sec × retention vs provisioned_disk and alert when projected fill <7d; monitor page_cache_hit_ratio <80% on brokers; alert on cross_region_replication_lag_bytes >1TB or replication_bandwidth_utilization >70% of link.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Versioning Log sits in this design For an S3-like store promising **read-after-write consistency, versioning, and eventual reclamation of deleted bytes**, the metadata service alone can't tell you *what happened and when*. It only tells you the current state: "this key points to these chunks." But several jobs in this system need the *history* of mutations — the garbage collector needs to know a DELETE happened 7 days ago so it can reclaim shards; cross-region replication needs an ordered stream of PUTs to replay remotely; billing needs per-hour size deltas; audit needs a tamper-evident trail. Rather than having each of those jobs poll the metadata tables (which would hammer a strongly-consistent SQL layer that's already on the critical path of every request), we emit one append-only event per mutation and let each consumer read the stream at its own pace. ## What happens without it If GC had to scan the metadata tables directly for tombstones, it would compete with user PUT/GET lookups on the same shards — users would see latency spikes whenever GC runs, and operators would see metadata CPU climb during sweep windows. Cross-region replication would either lag badly or amplify load 2×. Worse, deleted objects might never actually get reclaimed, so the 3 EB fleet silently grows into a storage leak. ## The numbers At **100K PUTs/sec + ~10K DELETEs/sec sustained**, that's ~110K events/sec × 86,400 sec/day ≈ **9.5 billion events/day**. Kafka easily absorbs this across partitioned topics, while forcing the SQL metadata layer to serve that as a change-feed would roughly double its write amplification. ## Trade-off One more system to operate (Kafka clusters, consumer lag monitoring) in exchange for decoupling four background jobs from the hot path.

gc.name: Garbage Collector
gc.summary: Background job that reclaims storage from tombstoned / expired / multipart-abandoned chunks.

sections.heading: What it reclaims
sections.body:
- Chunks whose metadata row is tombstoned and past the 7d grace window
- Orphaned multipart parts with upload_id expired (24h default)
- Old non-current versions after a lifecycle rule applies

sections.heading: Sweep algorithm
sections.body:
```
for shard in all_shards_on_disk: chunk_id = shard.chunk_id row = meta.get(chunk_id) if row is None or (row.tombstone and row.deleted_at < now - 7d): disk.delete(shard)
```
Runs continuously, throttled to <= 10% disk I/O so it doesn't compete with user traffic.

sections.heading: Safety
sections.body: Two-phase delete: GC first marks shard for removal (with 24h quarantine), then deletes. A stale metadata lookup during the quarantine window cannot cause a read miss because the shard file is still on disk.

bottlenecks.title: GC throughput can't keep pace with DELETE + lifecycle event rate
bottlenecks.trigger: Steady-state ~10K DELETEs/sec plus lifecycle expirations on 10T objects (even 0.01%/day = ~12K/sec) yields ~25K reclamation events/sec, each fanning out 9 quarantine RPCs = ~225K RPC/sec across data nodes. GC is throttled to ≤10% disk I/O per node, so effective reclamation rate is capped far below peak inflow during backup windows (300K PUT/sec feeding lifecycle expiries downstream).
bottlenecks.symptom: Kafka consumer lag on the `gc` group climbs from seconds to hours; `reclaimable_bytes` diverges from `reclaimed_bytes`; data-node disks fill despite user DELETEs completing successfully; eventually PUTs return 507 InsufficientStorage even though logical free space exists — a silent storage leak that becomes a user-visible outage.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Parallelize GC workers per Kafka partition (one worker per partition, scaled to match partition count) with idempotent quarantine keyed on (chunk_id, shard_idx); add a priority lane for events >5d old (approaching the 7d grace + Kafka retention edge); batch quarantine RPCs per data node (e.g., 1000 shards/RPC) to amortize network overhead; dynamically raise the I/O throttle to 25% when backlog > 1h.
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on `kafka_consumer_lag{group=gc} > 10M messages` or `> 1h time-lag`; alert when `reclaimable_bytes - reclaimed_bytes` trends positive over 24h; alert if `gc_events_consumed_per_sec / vlog_delete_events_per_sec < 0.95` sustained 10min; page immediately if any DELETE event is within 3d of Kafka 30d retention cutoff AND unprocessed.

bottlenecks.title: Full-fleet shard sweep scan cost grows unbounded with object count
bottlenecks.trigger: The sweep algorithm iterates `for shard in all_shards_on_disk` and does a metadata lookup per shard. With 10T objects × 9 shards = ~90T shards across 300K nodes = ~300M shards per node. Even at 10K metadata lookups/sec per GC worker (10% I/O budget), a full sweep of one node takes ~30,000 seconds (~8h); fleet-wide that's 300K nodes × millions of metadata RPCs = tens of billions of lookups per sweep cycle, hammering the 10K-node metadata tier.
bottlenecks.symptom: Metadata service sees a sustained baseline of GC-driven lookups competing with the 1M user GET/sec; metadata p99 latency creeps up during sweep windows; sweep cycle time grows faster than storage grows, so orphan shards (shards with no metadata row) accumulate indefinitely; bit-rot scrubber and GC compete for the same disk I/O budget.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Replace full-scan sweep with an event-driven model: GC primarily consumes the versioning log (tombstones + lifecycle events) and only runs a reconciliation sweep weekly at low priority; batch metadata lookups (e.g., 1000 chunk_ids per RPC using `WHERE chunk_id IN (...)`); use a bloom filter of live chunk_ids distributed to each data node so most shards are filtered locally without a metadata RPC; prioritize sweep of extents with highest tombstone density first.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `gc_metadata_lookup_qps` as fraction of total metadata QPS, alert if > 20%; alert on `sweep_cycle_duration_days > 14`; monitor `orphan_shard_ratio` (shards with no metadata row) per node — alert if > 0.1% or trending up.

bottlenecks.title: Multipart upload cleanup contention and orphan accumulation
bottlenecks.trigger: With 100K sustained PUTs/sec and 5% being multipart, a non-trivial fraction abandon (client crashes, network drops) — at 500K completes/day implies roughly 25K-50K abandoned upload_ids/day, each holding 10-1000 pending part rows pointing to real shards on data nodes. GC must sweep upload_ids >24h old and reclaim their part-referenced chunks; each cleanup is a cross-shard metadata transaction (pending_multipart rows + chunk quarantine) competing with CompleteMultipartUpload commits on the same rows.
bottlenecks.symptom: `pending_multipart` table grows unboundedly (5-10%/week) consuming metadata storage; abandoned multipart shards occupy data-node capacity invisibly (not counted as `reclaimable_bytes` until GC identifies them); cleanup transactions abort with retry errors under contention with live Complete operations; customer billing shows phantom storage usage they can't explain or delete.
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run a dedicated lightweight GC consumer on a timer (every 1h) that SELECTs `upload_id WHERE initiated_at < now - 24h LIMIT 10000` and quarantines referenced chunks in batches; co-locate cleanup with single-shard transactions by sharding pending_multipart on (bucket, key) same as objects table; expose `s3:AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` lifecycle rule and default it to 7d at bucket creation; emit a synthetic `LIFECYCLE_EXPIRE` event to the versioning log on cleanup so the main GC path handles shard reclamation uniformly.
bottlenecks.detection: Track `pending_multipart_rows` gauge — alert on >1%/day growth or absolute count > 10M; track `oldest_pending_upload_id_age_hours` — alert if > 48h (should never exceed 24h grace + 1h sweep); monitor `multipart_cleanup_txn_retry_rate` — alert if > 5%; reconcile `shards_referenced_by_pending_multipart` vs data-node-reported storage to catch drift.

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Garbage Collector sits in this S3-like design In this object store, DELETE doesn't actually delete anything on disk. The API writes a *tombstone* row in metadata and returns 204 — the user is happy in ~10ms. But the 9 erasure-coded shards for that object are still sitting on data nodes, taking up space. Same story for versioning: every PUT to an existing key creates a new version, and the old chunks linger. And multipart uploads that clients abandon halfway (network died, process crashed) leave orphan parts referencing real shards. Something has to walk through all this and actually free the bytes — that's the GC. It's separated from the DELETE path because reclaiming shards is slow, involves every data node holding a shard, and absolutely must not block a user request. ## What happens without it The fleet turns into a storage leak. Users DELETE happily, operators watch disk-free metrics shrink anyway, and eventually data nodes start rejecting PUTs with 507 InsufficientStorage even though "logically" there's tons of free space. Billing also breaks — customers see phantom usage for objects they thought they deleted. ## The numbers At **10 trillion objects with a 10:1 read:write ratio**, even a small DELETE rate (~10K/sec) means ~860M reclamation events per day, each fanning out to 9 shard deletions = **~7.7B shard-delete operations per day** across 300K data nodes. You cannot do that synchronously on the user's DELETE call; the GC amortizes it in the background, throttled to ≤10% disk I/O so user GETs keep their ~10ms latency. ## Trade-off Deletes are *logical*, not physical — you pay for the storage of deleted objects for up to ~7 days (grace window + quarantine) in exchange for fast, idempotent, crash-safe DELETEs.

operations.title: PUT object (multipart + erasure-coded replicate)
operations.name: PUT object (multipart + erasure-coded replicate)
operations.description: Client uploads a 500 MB object via multipart. Each part is EC-encoded into 6+3 shards and fanned out to data nodes across 3 AZs; metadata is committed only after write quorum.

steps.title: Client initiates multipart upload
steps.action: AWS SDK computes that 500 MB > 100 MB threshold, decides to do multipart with 50 MB part size (10 parts). Sends InitiateMultipartUpload first.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /my-bucket/datasets/2026-q1.parquet?uploads HTTP/1.1
Host: s3.example.com
Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 Credential=AKIA.../20260424/us-east-1/s3/aws4_request, SignedHeaders=host;x-amz-date, Signature=ab12...
x-amz-date: 20260424T101530Z
Content-Length: 0

steps.title: LB terminates TLS and picks API replica
steps.action: Initial InitiateMultipartUpload has no upload_id yet; routed via least-connections. Subsequent UploadPart calls will consistent-hash on the returned upload_id for stickiness.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.pick(algo="least_conn", healthy=True)
forward(req → upstream)

steps.title: Auth validates SigV4
steps.action: Auth service reconstructs canonical request and verifies the HMAC signature against the cached secret for access key AKIA.... Bucket policy check: caller has s3:PutObject on my-bucket.
steps.codeOrCommand:
canonical = build_canonical_request(req)
string_to_sign = f"AWS4-HMAC-SHA256\n{ts}\n{scope}\n{sha256(canonical)}"
expected_sig = hmac_sha256(derive_signing_key(secret), string_to_sign)
assert expected_sig == req.sig
policy_decision = evaluate(bucket_policy, iam_policy, op="s3:PutObject")
assert policy_decision == "Allow"

steps.title: API creates multipart upload id
steps.action: API generates a UUIDv7 upload_id, writes a pending-multipart marker to metadata, and returns upload_id to the client.

steps.title: Client uploads parts 1..10 in parallel
steps.action: SDK opens 8 concurrent UploadPart requests. We trace one (part 7) in detail; the others flow identically.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# Part 7 (of 10), 50 MB
PUT /my-bucket/datasets/2026-q1.parquet?partNumber=7&uploadId=01HZ8T7K4C-9f2a HTTP/1.1
Content-Length: 52428800
Content-MD5: a1b2c3d4...
x-amz-content-sha256: 9af3... <50 MB binary payload>

steps.title: API requests chunk placement from metadata
steps.action: API asks metadata service for 9 data-node placements (6 data + 3 parity) spread across 3 AZs. Placement returns specific (node_id, disk) tuples.
steps.codeOrCommand:
chunk_id = uuid7 # chunk_01HZ8T-7c11
placements = meta.allocate_placement( chunk_id=chunk_id, size=52428800, ec_k=6, ec_m=3, failure_domains=["az-1a", "az-1b", "az-1c"]
)
# → [
# {shard:0, node:"dn-8811", disk:3, az:"az-1a"},
# {shard:1, node:"dn-8823", disk:7, az:"az-1a"},
# {shard:2, node:"dn-9104", disk:2, az:"az-1a"},
# {shard:3, node:"dn-9301", disk:5, az:"az-1b"},
#...
# {shard:8, node:"dn-9902", disk:1, az:"az-1c"}
# ]

steps.title: Metadata service picks 9 placements
steps.action: Placement service consults capacity + health state of the fleet; picks 3 nodes per AZ that are under 80% full and not currently draining. Reserves capacity atomically so two concurrent allocations don't over-book the same disk.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT node_id, disk_id, az, free_bytes
FROM data_node_capacity
WHERE free_bytes > 52428800 * 2 AND status = 'ACTIVE' AND drain_at IS NULL
GROUP BY az
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
ORDER BY free_bytes DESC
LIMIT 9; -- 3 per AZ UPDATE data_node_capacity
SET reserved_bytes = reserved_bytes + 52428800
WHERE (node_id, disk_id) IN (...)

steps.title: Replication coordinator encodes and fans out
steps.action: API hands the 50 MB stream to the coordinator. Coordinator runs Reed-Solomon 6+3 and dispatches 9 PUT RPCs in parallel to the placed data nodes. Waits for write quorum of 6.
steps.decision: 9 of 9 acked in 42ms — quorum met. If we had seen < 6 acks within 2s: abort, surface 503 to client; replication coordinator would retry on a new placement.
steps.note: Parallel fan-out: p99 PUT latency is the 6th-fastest shard, not the slowest. This is the whole point of over-provisioning (9 shards for a 6-shard requirement).

steps.title: Data node writes shard to disk
steps.action: Each data node receives its shard, appends to its active extent file, updates the local index, fsyncs, and acks. This happens in parallel across all 9 nodes.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# On dn-9104, disk 2 (shard_idx=2)
extent = active_extent("/disk-02")
offset = extent.append(shard_bytes) # ~500 MB/s NVMe
extent.index_put("chunk_01HZ8T-7c11:2", ExtentRef(extent_id=extent.id, offset=offset, length=len(shard_bytes), crc32c=0x9a3f))
extent.fsync
return Ack(node="dn-9104", shard_idx=2, crc32c=0x9a3f)

steps.title: API returns part ETag to client
steps.action: Once the coordinator reports quorum, API commits the part's chunk_id into the pending-multipart metadata and returns the part's ETag (MD5 of the part bytes).

steps.title: Client collects all 10 ETags, sends CompleteMultipartUpload
steps.action: After all 10 parts ack, SDK issues the Complete call listing every part's number and ETag. This is what atomically makes the object visible for reads.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /my-bucket/datasets/2026-q1.parquet?uploadId=01HZ8T7K4C-9f2a HTTP/1.1
Content-Type: application/xml <CompleteMultipartUpload> <Part><PartNumber>1</PartNumber><ETag>"aa11..."</ETag></Part> <Part><PartNumber>2</PartNumber><ETag>"bb22..."</ETag></Part>... <Part><PartNumber>7</PartNumber><ETag>"a1b2c3d4..."</ETag></Part>... <Part><PartNumber>10</PartNumber><ETag>"jj99..."</ETag></Part>
</CompleteMultipartUpload>

steps.title: Metadata finalizes the object row
steps.action: Verify every listed ETag matches the stored part. Compute the composite ETag (MD5 of concatenated part MD5s, suffix -10). Commit a new version_id; clear the pending-multipart marker.

steps.title: Versioning log records the PUT
steps.action: Metadata service emits a CDC event into the versioning log stream (Kafka). Consumers: GC, cross-region replication, billing, audit.
steps.codeOrCommand:
producer.send( topic="object-events", key="my-bucket/datasets/2026-q1.parquet", value={ "ts": "2026-04-24T10:15:49.120Z", "op": "PUT", "bucket": "my-bucket", "key": "datasets/2026-q1.parquet", "version_id": "01HZ8TA-ver01", "size": 524288000, "actor": "arn:aws:iam::1234:user/alice" }
)

steps.title: API returns 200 OK with ETag and version id
steps.action: Final response; object is now GET-able with read-after-write consistency.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return Response(200, headers={ "ETag": '"d41d8cd9...-10"', "x-amz-version-id": "01HZ8TA-ver01" }, body=XML(CompleteMultipartUploadResult(...))
)

steps.title: SDK reports upload complete
steps.action: End-to-end PUT for a 500 MB multipart object: typically 3–8s over gigabit, bounded by client uplink rather than backend.

operations.title: GET object (metadata lookup → data node fan-in)
operations.name: GET object (metadata lookup → data node fan-in)
operations.description: Client downloads a 10 MB object. API resolves placement via metadata, fans out 6 parallel shard reads, reconstructs if any shard times out, streams bytes.

steps.title: Client issues GET
steps.action: Signed GET request. SDK is prepared to stream the response body directly to disk.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET /my-bucket/images/hero.png HTTP/1.1
Host: s3.example.com
Authorization: AWS4-HMAC-SHA256 Credential=AKIA.../20260424/us-east-1/s3/aws4_request...
x-amz-date: 20260424T101602Z

steps.title: LB forwards to API
steps.action: Least-connections; no stickiness needed for non-multipart reads.

steps.title: Auth validates SigV4 + policy
steps.action: Same signature check as PUT path; policy check is for s3:GetObject this time. Cached decision for this bucket+principal hits.
steps.codeOrCommand:
assert verify_sigv4(req)
policy_decision = evaluate(bucket_policy, iam_policy, op="s3:GetObject")
assert policy_decision == "Allow"

steps.title: API looks up object in metadata
steps.action: Fetch the current (non-tombstoned) version row for the key. Returns the chunk list and each chunk's shard placements.
steps.codeOrCommand:
row = meta.get_current_version("my-bucket", "images/hero.png")
# row.chunks = [
# {"chunk_id": "chunk_01HY-4a2b", "size": 10485760,
# "shards": [
# {"idx":0, "node":"dn-1041", "disk":5},
# {"idx":1, "node":"dn-1203", "disk":2},
#...
# {"idx":8, "node":"dn-2901", "disk":7}
# ]}
# ]

steps.title: Metadata returns placement
steps.action: Single-row read by (bucket, key) PK, latest version. Linearizable — reflects any completed PUT to this key (read-after-write).
steps.codeOrCommand:
SELECT version_id, size_bytes, etag, chunks
FROM objects
WHERE bucket = 'my-bucket' AND key = 'images/hero.png' AND tombstone = false
ORDER BY version_id DESC
LIMIT 1;

steps.title: Coordinator fans out shard reads
steps.action: Issue parallel reads to all 9 shard holders; need any 6 to reconstruct. Hedging: if the first 6 return in <100ms we skip the rest; if any one lags > 50ms past the 6th, we already have what we need.
steps.codeOrCommand:
futures = [data_node_rpc.get_async(p.node, p.disk, chunk_id, p.shard_idx) for p in placements] # 9 requests
shards_in = async for idx, bytes in as_completed(futures, needed=6, timeout_ms=500): shards_in.append((idx, bytes)) if len(shards_in) == 6: break
if len(shards_in) < 6: # try backup reads from rebuild-in-flight replicas, else 503 raise InsufficientShards
chunk_bytes = rs_decode(shards_in, k=6, m=3) # may reorder; handles missing indices
steps.decision: 6 of 9 shards arrived in 27ms — reconstruct and stream. If fewer than 6 arrive within 500ms: return 503 and let client retry; background re-replication will repair any stuck shards.

steps.title: Data node reads shard from disk
steps.action: Look up the shard in the local extent index, issue a pread, verify CRC32C, stream back. Hot shards are served from OS page cache (sub-ms); cold shards from NVMe (~5ms) or HDD (~40ms).
steps.codeOrCommand:
# On dn-1203, disk 2, shard_idx=1
ref = extent_index.get("chunk_01HY-4a2b:1")
# ExtentRef(extent=14921, offset=829104921, length=1747626, crc32c=0x4f82)
buf = pread(ref.extent_file, ref.offset, ref.length)
assert crc32c(buf) == ref.crc32c # bit-rot check
return buf
